newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU struggles to agree BSE beef aid package.
newsitem.headline: EU struggles to agree BSE beef aid package.

text.p: European Union farm ministers struggled on Wednesday to stitch together a package of measures to give extra aid for farmers hit by the mad cow crisis and to cut beef surpluses.

EU officials said ministers, on the third day of their meeting, generally welcomed a new Irish EU Presidency compromise calling for an extra 500 million Ecus ($635 million) aid to break a deadlock with the European Commission over compensation for beef farmers.
The aid would be on top of 850 million Ecus agreed by EU leaders in Florence in June.
Ireland later followed up with a proposal for distributing the aid between member states, with France, Germany and Britain receiving over half the total.
"There is the basis for a deal," said Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely.
But he warned that there was no new money available in the 1997 EU budget and that member states might find it difficult to agree on how the aid should be shared.
The crisis was triggered by a British government statement in March that the fatal cattle brain disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), might be transmitted to people.
EU beef demand has since fallen 15 percent and some 400,000 tonnes of unwanted beef have been put into storage.
Other changes in the latest compromise included a call for more money to fund a quality beef promotion scheme.
German demands to improve the terms of an EU scheme to cut output by marketing calves earlier and a higher premium for bulls were also met.
The compromise also reflected German wishes for a more balanced approach between extensive and intensive beef farming.
EU farm ministers unanimously rejected an initial Irish compromise on Tuesday, saying aid was insufficient and measures to cut beef surpluses unacceptable.
France, which had been the most critical, softened its stance on Wednesday, with a French official saying the new text was "negotiable."
Officials said only Portugal looked as if it would vote against the beef package because it wanted a bigger quota of male cattle eligible for EU aid.

The Irish presidency noted that 230 million Ecus of aid payable to beef producers in 1997 was brought forward to 1996 under an agreement drafted by EU farm ministers at an informal meeting in Killarney, Ireland, in September.
But Commission officials said 270 million Ecus in savings still had to be found in the 1997 budget.

The executive Commission previously argued that emergency aid agreed by EU leaders in Florence in June, topped up by national payments, would cover the livestock producers' estimated 1.2 billion Ecus losses in 1996.

Regarding aid in 1997 and 1998, Ireland has now suggested that 65 percent of around 1.3 billion Ecus aid due to oilseed farmers in 1997 be postponed until 1998, freeing more aid for livestock farmers.
Commission plans to slash payments to cash-rich cereal farmers to help pay for the beef package would be delayed until at least 1998 after opposition from nearly all member states.

An unpopular "Herod premium" for slaughtering new-born calves would be made optional with countries being able to choose instead a more expensive German scheme to encourage farmers to sell cattle earlier.
